newsitem.title: UK: IRA political arm refuses to join truce call for N. Ireland.
newsitem.headline: IRA political arm refuses to join truce call for N. Ireland.

text.p: The political arm of the Irish nationalist IRA guerrilla group refused to join in a call for an immediate truce in British-ruled Northern Ireland on Thursday but insisted it was trying to create conditions for one.

"The reality is that we do not have a ceasefire and we all have to work to create it," said Mitchell McLaughlin, chairman of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, as his party was plunged into a serious rift with the dominant nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), its rival for support among minority Catholics.
Political analysts said the row threatened to increase Sinn Fein's isolation from a flagging peace process which has seen doors closed to it in London, Dublin and Washington.

Responding to bitter criticism from SDLP leader John Hume, a key figure in attempts to achieve an end to decades of strife, McLaughlin said his party was "attempting to create conditions in which all political violence...will be eradicated."

In a BBC radio interview, he side-stepped Hume's call for Sinn Fein to demand an unconditional Irish Republican Army cessation but said: "We must make it very clear that we desire such an outcome and we believe we have a responsibility with others to create conditions in which it can happen..."

Hume, in his fiercest attack on republicans in recent years, said the Republican Movement, which comprises Sinn Fein and the IRA, had led its supporters down a "blind alley of violence" for more than 25 years in a campaign against British rule.

He also signalled that he was not prepared to continue talking indefinitely to Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams in the shadow of IRA violenc but a senior SDLP figure later denied Hume was distancing himself from peace-brokering talks with Adams.

In a hard-hitting article in the Belfast newspaper, The Irish News, the SDLP leader accused his republican rivals of electoral fraud and intimidation in "their bid to win the leadership of the northern (Ireland) nationalism".

"If the Sinn Fein leadership truly believe in what they say, then they must join with me today in publicly calling on the IRA for an immediate and unconditional end to a war which, by their own admission, has no purpose and cannot resolve this conflict or produce a lasting peace," he wrote.

The row comes at a time of tension in the run-up to a British general election in which majority pro-British Protestant and Catholic Irish parties are vying for the province's 18 seats in the British parliament.
Security sources said a suspected IRA attack was foiled in south Belfast early on Thursday. Two men were arrested and two assault rifles and a grenade were siezed.
